Probably yes—but it may be challenging.

The Moon is 6.78° above the eastern horizon, at azimuth 104° (roughly east-southeast), and 97% illuminated. Its angular size is about 0.52°, so it is physically large and nearly full. Under a clear sky, an ordinary observer can often see a nearly full Moon in daylight, especially when it is that bright.

The main difficulties are:

- **Very low altitude:** atmospheric haze, buildings, trees, and terrain can obscure it.
- **Bright sky:** daylight reduces contrast, though a nearly full Moon remains bright enough to stand out.
- **Sun direction:** the Sun is only about 160° away, so the Moon is well away from the Sun and should not be lost in glare. Keep the Sun out of your view and never scan near it.
- **Twilight timing:** with the Sun only 3° above the horizon, the sky is still bright, but the Moon may become easier to see as the Sun sets.

So, if your eastern-southeastern horizon is unobstructed and reasonably clear, I’d expect you to be able to spot it—possibly with some deliberate searching, but not requiring binoculars. Look about 7° above the horizon, roughly four Moon-widths above it, at azimuth 104°.
